standard.title: Data as pictures, numbers and words
standard.description: represent data as pictures, symbols, numbers and words
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can represent data using objects, pictures and symbols (AC9TDIFK02). They have matched physical objects and pictures to what they represent. They have not yet worked with multiple simultaneous representation forms (words, numbers, symbols, pictures) or reasoned about equivalence across forms.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students represent the same data using different forms — pictures, symbols, numbers and words — and recognise that different forms can convey equivalent information.

nodes.label: Recognising representation forms
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify data represented as pictures, symbols, numbers and words and name which form is being used
nodes.minimum_width: Given examples of data in different forms, correctly identify each as a picture, symbol, number or word
nodes.typical_width: Identify data represented in all four forms across a range of familiar examples (class attendance tally, weather icons, temperature numbers, written labels); explain what information each conveys
wider: Examine First Nations Australians' seasonal calendars where pictures represent connected events and resource availability — identify what data each picture represents and compare to word or number forms of the same information
Explore how the same phoneme can be represented by different letter combinations in written words — connecting data representation to literacy

response_modes.reason: Students need to accumulate a range of examples of each representation form — a single example of 'a number represents data' is not sufficient to build a reliable category. Repeated encounters across varied contexts (weather, calendar, classroom data) build the recognition repertoire.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The First Nations seasonal calendar direction is genuinely rich — it connects data representation to culturally situated knowledge systems where pictures carry precise data meaning, making the 'pictures represent data' concept concrete and cross-cultural.
success_criteria: Correctly identifies at least three representation forms from examples
States what information each example conveys
nodes.hinge_reason: Without a recognition repertoire for all four representation forms, Node 2 (representing the same data in multiple forms) lacks the raw material — students cannot produce forms they cannot yet reliably identify.

nodes.label: Representing the same data in different forms
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can represent the same data using more than one form — for example representing a count as a tally, a number and a word
nodes.minimum_width: Represent one piece of data in at least two different forms (e.g. draw a picture and write a number for the same quantity)
nodes.typical_width: Represent the same data (e.g. class pet vote results, weather observation, attendance count) in three or more forms — picture, tally/number, word, and symbol — and explain that the forms show the same information
wider: Create a class data display using different representation forms for the same dataset — for example representing favourite foods as a picture graph, a tally chart and a written sentence
Explore how a tally mark and a digit are both ways to represent numbers — count the same collection using both and compare

response_modes.reason: Students often treat different representation forms as containing different information rather than equivalent information. Encountering the same data in multiple forms across several contexts (not just one) helps build the equivalence understanding — the data is the same, only the representation changes.

success_criteria: Represents one piece of data in at least two distinct forms correctly
Conveys the same information in both forms — the representation is equivalent, not different data
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who still treat different representation forms as containing different information (rather than equivalent information) cannot reason about why forms are chosen in Node 3 — the equivalence understanding must be present before purpose-of-form reasoning can proceed.

nodes.label: Recognising equivalence across forms
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can recognise that different representation forms — pictures, symbols, numbers and words — can convey the same data, and explain why different forms may be used
nodes.minimum_width: Given two different representations of the same data (e.g. a picture and a word), confirm they represent the same thing and suggest one reason why each form might be used
nodes.typical_width: Compare several representations of the same dataset; explain that the forms are equivalent and give examples of when each form is most useful (e.g. pictures for quick understanding, numbers for precise counting, words for explaining)
wider: Investigate why First Nations Australians use pictures in seasonal calendars rather than words or numbers — discuss what a picture form conveys that words or numbers might not
Compare how numbers are spelled the same way regardless of accent (spoken form varies, written form is fixed) — connecting representation stability to the purpose of standardised forms

response_modes.reason: Reasoning about why different forms are used requires students to think about the purpose of representation, not just recognise forms. Scaffolding the reasoning (who is using it? what do they need to know? which form makes that easiest?) prevents students from treating form choice as arbitrary.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The First Nations seasonal calendar direction is rich at this node — discussing why picture form is used (not just that it is used) surfaces the purposeful nature of representation choice, making the concept of data representation genuinely thoughtful rather than procedural.
success_criteria: Confirms two different representations of the same data are equivalent
Gives at least one reason why each representation form might be useful
